title: The Rhine Journeys of the Sibyl: the Anchorage, the Living Light, and the Roads No Abbess Rode
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bermersheim vor der Höhe, the tenth child
stops.date_confidence: year attested; birthplace disputed. Most modern sources give Bermersheim vor der Höhe, where the baptismal church stands; the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 names Böckelheim on the Nahe instead. German Wikipedia states plainly that the exact birthplace is contested.
stops.campa: A tenth child is born to a family of free noble rank in the vineyard country between Alzey and the Nahe. The village keeps the baptismal church and claims the rest; another tradition puts the house forty kilometres west, on the Nahe itself. She is given, as tenth children were given, to God. Much later she will write that before her bones and veins were fully strengthened she was already seeing a light, and that she asked one of her nurses whether she saw it too, and was afraid at the answer.
stops.quote: Up to my fifteenth year I saw much, and related some of the things seen to others, who would inquire with astonishment, whence such things might come.
stops.quote_source: Hildegard's autobiographical fragment, preserved in her Vita, as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), translator unnamed
suggested_refs: The parish church of Bermersheim vor der Höhe, site of her baptism

stops.name: Disibodenberg, given to the anchoress
stops.date_confidence: contested. The Vita gives her age as eight, which yields 1106; several modern scholars argue for about fourteen, counting back from the formal enclosure of 1112. Both readings are in print and neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: She is handed to Jutta von Sponheim, a count's daughter who has chosen to be walled up rather than married. The Vita says the child is eight. Others count back from the enclosure and make her fourteen. Either way the transaction is the ordinary one of the age: a noble daughter delivered to a hill above the Glan, to a woman who will teach her the psalter, enough Latin to sing it, and a life measured out in hours. The hill belongs to a monastery of men. The cell they wall the women into will outgrow the arrangement the men made for it.
sources: Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, as summarized in Wikipedia, 'Hildegard of Bingen'
suggested_refs: The ruins of Disibodenberg above Odernheim am Glan

stops.name: Disibodenberg, the stone closed on All Saints' Day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the Vita and Wikipedia agree that the vows were received by Bishop Otto of Bamberg on All Saints Day 1112
stops.campa: The rite is read over them as over the dead. Jutta and Hildegard are enclosed in a cell built against the wall of the monks' church, and Bishop Otto of Bamberg receives their vows. The cell has a window for food and a window on the altar. Through the first they are fed; through the second they hear Mass and can be heard singing. Other daughters of the nobility ask to be shut in with them, and the anchorage meant for two becomes, within twenty years, a community with a rule and a library.
sources: Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, cited via Wikipedia, 'Hildegard of Bingen'
suggested_refs: The foundations of the women's enclosure against the monks' church at Disibodenberg

stops.name: Disibodenberg, elected magistra
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Jutta dies after twenty-four years in the cell, and the women elect Hildegard to lead them. She is thirty-eight and has spent all but her childhood behind that wall. The office is magistra, mistress of the women, subordinate to the abbot of the monks who own the hill, the ground, the bread, and the dowries the novices bring with them. She teaches, she governs a dozen women, she reads what the monk Volmar carries in to her, and she says nothing to anyone about the light.
suggested_refs: The grave of Jutta von Sponheim at Disibodenberg

stops.name: Disibodenberg, the command to write
stops.date_confidence: attested; the year is given in her own Protestificatio to Scivias
stops.campa: In her forty-third year a light comes and the sense of the scriptures opens inside it, and a voice tells her to say and write what she sees and hears. She refuses, out of doubt and modesty and fear of what men will say, until sickness pins her to a bed. Then she takes the sickness as a scourge, calls for Volmar, and begins to dictate. The nun Richardis von Stade helps her. The book will be called Scivias, Know the Ways, and it will take her ten years to finish.
stops.quote: Cry out, therefore, and write thus!
stops.quote_source: Scivias, Protestificatio, trans. Columba Hart and Jane Bishop (Paulist Press, 1990)
suggested_refs: The Protestificatio, her own account of the 1141 commission

stops.name: Disibodenberg, the letter to Bernard of Clairvaux
stops.date_confidence: dated c.1146-47 in the standard letter collections; the translation quoted here is reproduced on Wikiquote with no translator named
stops.campa: Uncertain of her own visions, she writes to the most formidable churchman alive. Bernard of Clairvaux can make a thing orthodox or heresy across Latin Europe with a sentence. She tells him she is disturbed by what has appeared to her, seen not with fleshly eyes but only in the spirit, and asks whether she should speak or keep silent. He answers briefly and warmly and tells her to accept the grace. He is also the teacher of the man now sitting on the throne of Peter, and that will matter within two years.
stops.quote: Father, I am greatly disturbed by a vision which has appeared to me through divine revelation, a vision seen not with my fleshly eyes but only in my spirit.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Bernard of Clairvaux, c. 1146-47, translated excerpt reproduced on Wikiquote, translator unnamed
sources: The Letters of Hildegard of Bingen, trans. Baird and Ehrman (cited, not consulted)
suggested_refs: Bernard's reply to Hildegard, in the Baird and Ehrman letter edition

stops.name: Trier, the synod hears Scivias read aloud
stops.date_confidence: the synod ran November 1147 to February 1148; sources cite the episode as 1147 or 1148 without distinguishing
stops.campa: Pope Eugene III winters at Trier for a synod, and the unfinished Scivias is carried to him. Passages are read aloud to the assembled bishops. The pope sends the nun at Disibodenberg a letter of blessing and permission to publish whatever she receives in vision. The letter is a routine act of chancery. Its effect is that a woman of the empire now holds written papal authority to speak in public about whatever she is shown, and she keeps the letter by her for the rest of her life.
sources: Hildegard, 'Letter 4', in The Letters of Hildegard of Bingen, trans. Baird and Ehrman, pp. 34-35
suggested_refs: The letter of Eugene III to Hildegard, Letter 4 in the Baird and Ehrman edition

stops.name: Disibodenberg, the abbot refuses to let them go
stops.date_confidence: the resistance and the eventual release are attested; the causal detail, Abbot Kuno objecting over prestige and dowries and yielding to a paralysis read as divine pressure, comes from the Vita, a canonization document with an interest in the miracle, and is tradition
stops.campa: She announces that she has been shown a place: the Rupertsberg, a bare hill where the Nahe empties into the Rhine, and that her women are to go there. The abbot refuses. The women are the monastery's prestige and their families' dowries are its income. She falls ill and cannot be moved from her bed. The monks who wrote her life report that the abbot understood the paralysis and gave way. What stands outside their account is that he resisted, and that in the end he released them.
suggested_refs: The chapter house of Disibodenberg, where the release was negotiated

stops.name: Rupertsberg, twenty women arrive at a ruin
stops.date_confidence: attested; note that Wikipedia's Disibodenberg article says the women relocated in 1147, against the mainstream 1150, and this internal tension is unresolved
stops.campa: About twenty women come down off the hill and cross to a ruin above Bingen where an old church of Saint Rupert stands. There is no water at first. Archbishop Heinrich of Mainz backs the foundation and the families of the nuns pay for it. Volmar comes with them as provost and scribe, leaving his own house to follow the woman whose sentences he has been writing down for nine years. Some of the women weep for what has been left behind. Hildegard builds workshops in stone and pipes water into the house.
suggested_refs: The surviving vaulted cellar of Rupertsberg near Bingerbrück, most of what is left of the convent

stops.name: Rupertsberg, Scivias finished
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's Hildegard article dates completion 1151; its Scivias article gives 1151 or 1152. The contradiction stands.
stops.campa: Ten years after the voice, the book is done: twenty-six visions in three parts. She has illuminations made to go with the text, laid on by hands working in her own house under her direction, not by her own hand. The manuscript is copied and it travels. Bishops write to her now, and abbesses, and eventually the emperor. Copies go out to houses she has never seen. The letters that come back do not ask whether her visions are genuine; they ask her to settle questions their writers cannot settle themselves.
stops.quote: But I, though I saw and heard these things, refused to write for a long time through doubt and bad opinion and the diversity of human words, not with stubbornness but in the exercise of humility, until, laid low by the scourge of God, I fell upon a bed of sickness.
stops.quote_source: Scivias, Protestificatio, trans. Columba Hart and Jane Bishop (Paulist Press, 1990)
suggested_refs: The Rupertsberg Scivias codex, illuminated under her direction and lost in 1945

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the Ordo Virtutum
stops.date_confidence: dated to the years of the move and construction; the performance occasion is not documented
stops.campa: Amid the building she writes a play to be sung. A soul is pulled between the Virtues and the Devil, and her nuns take the parts. It is among the oldest surviving morality plays, and the only musical drama of the Middle Ages whose words and whose music are both credited to one named person. In the same years she assembles the Symphonia, a cycle of her own liturgical songs, so that the house she has built out of a ruin sings nothing at its hours that she has not written for it.
sources: The Dendermonde and Wiesbaden Riesencodex manuscripts of the Symphonia
suggested_refs: The Riesencodex at Wiesbaden, carrying the Symphonia and the Ordo Virtutum

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the chapel consecrated
stops.date_confidence: the consecration by Archbishop Henry of Mainz in 1152 is attested. Whether the Ordo Virtutum was performed at this dedication is only a possibility in the sources, repeated until it hardened, and is tradition.
stops.campa: Archbishop Henry of Mainz consecrates the convent chapel. The community that left Disibodenberg with nothing now has a church, a scriptorium, workshops, and its own water. The music sung to him that day is hers. She has written what her women sing at every hour, in a line unlike the plainchant of the age, with leaps and long melismas that climb past where a trained singer expects to stop. The women performing it for the archbishop learned it from her, in this house, and it is sung nowhere else.
suggested_refs: The consecration of the Rupertsberg chapel by Archbishop Henry of Mainz, 1152

segments.name: The Green Physic and the Letters

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the letters go out
stops.date_confidence: the correspondence runs across three decades; 1152 is a marker for its opening rather than a dated event
stops.campa: Letters leave the Rupertsberg and letters come back. She writes to Elisabeth of Schönau, a younger visionary a day's ride away who is being doubted as she was doubted. She writes to popes, to abbots, to bishops she rebukes by name, to the emperor, and to laypeople who want to know whether a dream meant anything. She calls herself a poor little figure of a woman and then tells archbishops what the Living Light says about their negligence, and they write back asking for more.
sources: The Letters of Hildegard of Bingen, trans. Baird and Ehrman (cited, not consulted)
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Hildegard and Elisabeth of Schönau

stops.name: Rupertsberg, Physica and Causae et Curae
stops.date_confidence: undatable. No colophon fixes either work; the 1150s are a scholarly estimate, and the research pool's own two lenses disagreed on whether the dating is attested or reconstructed.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years she compiles two books with nothing visionary in them. The Physica sorts plants, elements, trees, stones, fish, birds, and beasts by what they do to a human body. The Causae et Curae treats the body itself, its humors, its illnesses, its conception, its melancholy. No vision is cited as her authority anywhere in either. She simply states what a thing does. Nothing in these pages asks a reader to believe her about anything except the plants.
stops.quote: It happens that certain men suffer diverse illnesses. This comes from the phlegm which is superabundant within them.
sources: Physica and Causae et Curae manuscripts
suggested_refs: The Physica, her natural history of what heals and what harms

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the Book of Life's Merits
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The second visionary book: the Liber Vitae Meritorum, in which the vices step forward and speak in their own voices and are answered by the virtues opposed to them. It is a court, and everything in it is argued rather than asserted. In the same year Archbishop Arnold of Mainz seals the charters fixing the convent's property and legal standing, and the house that began as a roofless ruin becomes an institution able to hold land, take novices, and outlive the woman who built it.
suggested_refs: The charters of Archbishop Arnold of Mainz establishing Rupertsberg, 1158

stops.name: Mainz, the boat upriver at sixty
stops.date_confidence: attested as the first of four tours; the individual stops are reconstructed from her letters and from her biographer Theodoric rather than from dated documents
stops.campa: At sixty she leaves the enclosure. No abbess of the empire has done this. She travels with her archbishop's licence and the eleven-year-old letter of Eugene III behind her, takes a boat where the Main comes into the Rhine, and goes up into Franconia to preach. Her biographer Theodoric will count twenty-one places where she preached, five of them cathedral cities. Her subject is not consolation. It is the negligence of the clergy and the chastisement coming to a church grown fat and dull.
sources: Academic summaries of Theodoric's account of the preaching tours
suggested_refs: Theodoric's list of the twenty-one places where Hildegard preached

stops.name: Würzburg, preaching to the clergy on the Main
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stop on the first tour; the day and the order of the Franconian towns are reconstructed
stops.campa: She preaches to the clergy of Würzburg, in a diocese where a woman addressing priests in chapter has neither precedent nor procedure. She does not claim the office of preacher. She claims to report: the Living Light says this, and she says what it says, and that distinction is what keeps her inside the law while she does the thing the law forbids. The letters surviving from Franconian clergy afterward ask her for copies, for interpretations, and for a word about their own souls.
suggested_refs: Hildegard's surviving letters to the clergy of Würzburg

stops.name: Ebrach, before the monks of Bernard's order
stops.date_confidence: attested through her correspondence with Ebrach; the position within the tour is reconstructed
stops.campa: At the Cistercian house of Ebrach in the Steigerwald she preaches to monks of Bernard's own order, twelve years after writing to Bernard to ask whether she was mad. The correspondence with Ebrach survives. The abbot addresses her as an authority, and she answers in the register she has perfected by now: the vision reported flatly, in the present tense, with no apology and no argument, and then the application to the men in front of her, which is never flattering.
sources: Itinerary reconstruction in the standard biographies
suggested_refs: The Cistercian abbey church of Ebrach

stops.name: Bamberg, the eastern limit
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The extension of the first tour to Bamberg is a reconstruction by modern biographers and is not fixed by a dated primary source.
stops.campa: The first tour is carried as far as Bamberg, the cathedral city on the Regnitz, the easternmost ground she reaches. No dated document puts her there. Her presence rests on the letters and on Theodoric's count of twenty-one places, and it may be wrong. From Bamberg the boat turns and comes back down the Main and the Rhine to Bingen. She goes back inside the walls she has lived behind since she was a child, having been out of them for a season. Within two years she leaves again, westward this time, up the Moselle.
sources: Traditional itinerary reconstruction by modern biographers
suggested_refs: Bamberg cathedral, easternmost point of the first preaching tour

segments.name: Second Tour: the Moselle and the Saar

stops.name: Trier, preaching where the pope read her book
stops.date_confidence: attested as the second tour in the chronology followed here; the research pool's geography lens instead labelled the Rhineland circuit the second tour, and that disagreement is recorded in the report
stops.campa: Two years later she goes west, up the Moselle to Trier, the city where a pope had her unfinished book read aloud thirteen years before. She preaches there to clergy and people. What survives from Trier is an accounting: the age is womanish, the priests are asleep, and the justice of God is not asleep. Trier is the oldest city in Germany and has heard a great deal in its time. It has not heard this from a woman of sixty-two standing where a bishop is supposed to stand.
sources: Academic summaries of Theodoric's account of the preaching tours
suggested_refs: Hildegard's Trier sermon, preserved among her letters

stops.name: Metz, into the kingdom
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Metz appears in the reconstructed Lorraine itinerary but is not fixed by a dated letter. The research pool wrongly assigned it to a fourth tour in 1170.
stops.campa: The Lorraine circuit carries her to Metz on the Seille, in the kingdom rather than the empire, where the bishop is a great lord and the burghers are already restive under him. She preaches; the visit is held by the reconstructed itinerary rather than by any dated letter. She is travelling by river and by cart, in her sixties, in a body that has been sick since childhood, into cities where the only other women speaking in public are being burned in the same decades.
sources: Traditional itinerary reconstruction in the modern biographies
suggested_refs: The cathedral precinct of Metz in the twelfth century

stops.name: Krauftal, a house of women in the Vosges
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and the coordinate is a low-confidence regional estimate rather than a located building. The identification of the addressee community rests on a letter whose recipient scholars dispute.
stops.campa: In Alsace she is held to have preached at Krauftal, to a community of women living under the Rule. The place cannot be securely located. The identification rests on a single letter whose addressee scholars argue over, and what can honestly be given for it is a district in the Vosges foothills, not a road and a house. The western circuit ends here: Trier, then Metz, then a community of women in the hills, the furthest west she goes, and the one audience in four tours made up entirely of women.
sources: Hildegard's correspondence with a convent identified by some scholars as Krauftal; identification disputed
suggested_refs: The disputed Krauftal letter and the question of its recipient

stops.name: Boppard, the collegiate church on the great road
stops.date_confidence: the Rhineland circuit is variously dated 1161 to 1163, and the research pool's two lenses disagreed on whether it is the second or the third tour. The chronology followed here makes it the third.
stops.campa: The third circuit goes down the Rhine, the great road of the empire, past every toll castle between Bingen and Cologne, where the water is narrow and the tolls are the reason the castles are there at all. At Boppard she preaches at the collegiate church of Saint Severus. The town is imperial property and answers to no bishop, so there is no bishop in it who can forbid her the pulpit. How long the whole circuit takes is not agreed anywhere: the accounts allow a single season on the water, or three years of them.
suggested_refs: The collegiate church of Saint Severus at Boppard

stops.name: Andernach, the quay and the millstones
stops.date_confidence: tradition; not confirmed by any surviving dated letter
stops.campa: Downstream at Andernach, where the volcanic country begins and the millstones of the Eifel are shipped from the quay, tradition puts her among the clergy. No dated letter confirms it. The Rhine towns of the middle valley sit close enough together that a boat can make several in a week, and the reconstructed itinerary reads like the schedule of a visitation rather than of a pilgrimage: church, chapter, sermon, and on downstream with the current before the light goes.
suggested_refs: The Rhine quay at Andernach, shipping point of the Eifel millstone trade

stops.name: Siegburg, the Michaelsberg
stops.date_confidence: attested through her correspondence with the abbey; position in the tour reconstructed
stops.campa: At the Michaelsberg above Siegburg she preaches to the Benedictines of a reforming house founded by an archbishop of Cologne. The correspondence with Siegburg survives. She is a Benedictine addressing Benedictines, which makes this the one setting on the whole circuit where her presence needs no defending, and she uses it: fifty years under the Rule qualify her to tell these monks precisely what the Rule has cost her, and what she considers it to have been worth.
sources: Hildegard's correspondence with the abbey of Siegburg
suggested_refs: Michaelsberg Abbey above Siegburg

stops.name: Werden, the northern limit on the Ruhr
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and disputed among biographers as to whether Werden belongs to this circuit or a later one
stops.campa: The northernmost point of her travelling life is the abbey at Werden on the Ruhr, founded by a Frisian missionary four centuries earlier and grown rich on Westphalian corn. Biographers disagree about which tour it belongs to. It stands roughly two hundred and fifty kilometres by water from her own house, which for a woman past sixty who has been ill since infancy is a fact worth stating without ornament. No account of the return journey survives.
sources: Traditional itinerary reconstruction; tour assignment disputed
suggested_refs: Werden Abbey on the Ruhr, founded by Saint Ludger

stops.name: Cologne, the sermon against the Cathars
stops.date_confidence: the sermon is generally placed in 1163 by scholarship, while the research pool's chronology lens dated the Rhine circuit to 1161 and its geography lens to 1160. The contradiction is unresolved.
stops.campa: At Cologne, the largest city north of the Alps, she preaches to the cathedral clergy against the Cathars spreading through the Rhineland. Her argument is not primarily about the heretics. It is that the heretics have succeeded because the clergy are slack, and that a people follows whoever appears to be living cleanly. Her biographer records it as an unusually forceful sermon for a woman to deliver. It survives because the clergy of Cologne wrote to her afterward and asked her to send them a copy.
sources: Hildegard's letter to the clergy of Cologne
suggested_refs: Hildegard's Cologne sermon, sent to the cathedral clergy at their own request

stops.name: Ingelheim, before the emperor
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and sharply contested. Sources variously give 1150, 1154, and 1163, and at least one questions whether a face-to-face meeting occurred at all, since the evidence is a letter of the emperor's whose authenticity is doubted.
stops.campa: At the imperial palace at Ingelheim, downstream from her own house, tradition sets a meeting between the abbess and Frederick Barbarossa. The evidence is a letter whose authenticity is questioned, and three different years are given for an encounter one source doubts happened. The record is firmer afterward: an imperial letter of protection for the Rupertsberg, and a correspondence in which she warns the emperor, plainly and repeatedly, against the antipopes he is sustaining.
sources: Conflicting German and English secondary accounts of the Ingelheim meeting
suggested_refs: The imperial letter of protection issued to Rupertsberg by Barbarossa's court

segments.name: The Book of Divine Works, and Swabia at Seventy

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the largest book begun
stops.date_confidence: attested as begun 1163; completion cited variously as 1172, 1173, or 1174
stops.campa: She begins the third and largest of the visionary books, the Liber Divinorum Operum, and it will occupy her for ten years. Its subject is the cosmos and the place of a human being inside it. The wheels of the world turn within a human shape; winds are breath and rivers are veins and the firmament is a skull. It is a physiology of everything, written by the woman who has already written a physiology of the body, and the two books do not contradict each other anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Lucca manuscript of the Liber Divinorum Operum with its illuminated cosmic figures

stops.name: Eibingen, the second house across the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Rupertsberg is full. She takes a ruined house across the Rhine at Eibingen, above Rüdesheim, and settles a second community in it under a prioress, keeping the government of both houses in her own hands. In her late sixties she crosses the river regularly to teach there. This is the convent that will outlast the other by four and a half centuries, and the one that will take her bones in when the first is burned by an army she could not have imagined.
suggested_refs: The site of the medieval Eibingen convent below the present Abtei St. Hildegard

stops.name: Rupertsberg, three years down
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the episode is reported in later accounts of her life and is not independently dated with precision
stops.campa: She is ill for something near three years. She has been ill all her life, and the pattern she herself sets down is that the visions arrive with pain and the pain lifts when she obeys them, which her biographers then repeat until it becomes the argument for her authenticity. The dates of this collapse are not fixed anywhere. She is close to seventy. She dictates through it, governs two houses through it, and comes out of it to make the longest journey of her life.
sources: Secondary biographical summaries of Hildegard's illnesses
suggested_refs: The infirmary of Rupertsberg

stops.name: Maulbronn, the fourth tour turns south
stops.date_confidence: attested through her correspondence with Maulbronn. The research pool wrongly dated this visit 1163 and called it a third tour; the Swabian circuit is the fourth, in 1170.
stops.campa: The fourth tour goes south into Swabia, country she has never seen, and she is in her early seventies. At the Cistercian abbey of Maulbronn, whose monks are raising the cloister that will still be standing eight hundred years later, she preaches and corresponds. She travels by cart now. The distance from Bingen is more than two hundred kilometres overland, away from the rivers that carried her on the first three circuits, and she covers it in a body she has never once described as strong.
suggested_refs: The Cistercian abbey of Maulbronn, under construction at the time of her visit

stops.name: Hirsau, the reform abbey in the Black Forest
stops.date_confidence: tradition; not attested by a dated letter. The coordinate here corrects a value in circulation that lies about fourteen kilometres south, in open country near Nagold.
stops.campa: At Hirsau in the Black Forest, the reforming abbey whose customs half the monasteries of Germany have copied, tradition places her among the monks. No dated letter fixes the visit. The Hirsau reform had restored, among other things, the double house of men and women under one abbot, which is the arrangement she spent forty years escaping at Disibodenberg. She arrives as the head of two independent houses of her own, invited, with a papal licence in her baggage.
suggested_refs: The Hirsau customs and their spread through the German reform monasteries

stops.name: Kirchheim unter Teck, the priest who asked for it in writing
stops.date_confidence: tradition as to the visit; the letter to Werner of Kirchheim is associated with this journey. The research pool wrongly dated the stop 1163.
stops.campa: At Kirchheim unter Teck, below the Swabian Alb, she preaches to a congregation whose priest, Werner, afterward writes and asks her to send him what she said. She sends it. The letter that survives is the harshest thing she ever addressed to clergy: an image of the Church herself, disfigured and complaining, and an indictment of priests who handle the sacrament with dirty hands and worse lives. They asked for the text. They kept it. It is preserved because of them.
sources: Hildegard's letter to Werner of Kirchheim
suggested_refs: Hildegard's letter to Werner of Kirchheim, requested by its recipient

stops.name: Zwiefalten, the last house on the last road
stops.date_confidence: attested through her correspondence with Zwiefalten Abbey. The research pool misdated it to 1160-61 and called it a third tour.
stops.campa: Zwiefalten, in the Swabian Jura, is the last house on the last journey, and the correspondence with its Benedictines survives. From here the road turns north again toward the Rhine and the travelling stops for good. She is seventy-two. The nine years remaining belong to the scriptorium, to two convents, and to one long fight with the archdiocese of Mainz. Four tours have covered ground no enclosed woman of her century covered, on the licence of a pope nineteen years dead.
suggested_refs: Zwiefalten Abbey in the Swabian Jura

stops.name: Rupertsberg, Volmar dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Volmar dies. He has been her provost, her scribe, and her editor for more than thirty years: the man who took Scivias down word by word while she lay ill, who left his own monastery to follow her women to a ruin, who corrected her Latin without touching her sense. She writes that she has lost the one man who understood her. The monks of Disibodenberg refuse for a time to send a replacement. Guibert of Gembloux comes later, and proves far more interested in her than she is in him.
suggested_refs: Volmar of Disibodenberg, provost and scribe of Rupertsberg

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the last book finished and the light described
stops.date_confidence: completion of the Liber Divinorum Operum is cited variously as 1172, 1173, or 1174; the letters to Guibert quoted here are dated 1175 and 1176
stops.campa: The Book of Divine Works is finished, ten years in the making, the last of the three. Writing to Guibert she describes at last, and precisely, what has been happening to her since infancy. She calls it the shadow of the Living Light. It occupies no space, and it is brighter than a cloud carrying the sun. She sees it while she is awake, with her eyes open, and reads words and figures inside it. She has never been in ecstasy, she insists, and has never once lost consciousness while it lasts.
stops.quote: The light which I see thus is not spatial, but it is far, far brighter than a cloud which carries the sun.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Guibert of Gembloux (1175), as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Hildegard of Bingen'
suggested_refs: Hildegard's letters to Guibert of Gembloux, the fullest account of her visionary faculty

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the grave in the convent cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A young nobleman who had been excommunicated, and who was reconciled and absolved before he died, is buried in the convent cemetery. The clergy of Mainz demand that the body be dug up. Hildegard, eighty years old, refuses. The archbishop's officials then place the Rupertsberg under interdict: no Mass, no communion, and no singing of the Office. The house she built to sing her own music at every hour of the day and night is ordered into silence, and she does not open the grave.
suggested_refs: The convent cemetery of Rupertsberg

stops.name: Mainz, the letter on the burial and the singing
stops.date_confidence: attested that she wrote in protest and produced witnesses, and that the interdict was lifted shortly before her death. A claim in circulation that it ran two years is wrong: the episode belongs to the last year of her life, roughly autumn 1178 to spring 1179.
stops.campa: She writes to the prelates of Mainz. Her defence of the burial is legal: she produces witnesses that the man died absolved, and no penalty can follow a body already reconciled. Her defence of the singing is not legal at all. She argues that praise sung aloud is what the body was made for, that silencing it is the devil's proper work, and that men who impose silence on a house of God without cause should consider what company they will keep. The interdict is lifted within months.
sources: Hildegard's letter to the prelates of Mainz
suggested_refs: Hildegard's letter to the Mainz prelates defending the burial and the sacredness of music

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the seventeenth of September
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to the day, aged about eighty-one. The two crosses of light reported over the convent are a miracle account from the Vita and are tradition; one lens of this research pool wrongly tagged them as attested.
stops.campa: She dies at the Rupertsberg on the seventeenth of September, eighty-one years old, having outlived the pope who licensed her, the archbishop who consecrated her chapel, and the scribe who wrote her books. Her sisters report two arcs of light appearing in the night sky above the convent and crossing over the room where she lay. The interdict is lifted in the spring. The house sings the Office over her body, which it could not lawfully have done six months before.
suggested_refs: The Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, compiled by Godfrey of Disibodenberg and Theoderic of Echternach

stops.name: Rupertsberg, the Swedish fire
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Swedish troops of the Thirty Years' War sack and burn the Rupertsberg. The house has stood four hundred and eighty years. What is left standing is sold off and pulled down in the nineteenth century, and later building goes over the ground, so that a vaulted cellar is most of what survives of the convent she piped water into with her own arrangements. The community does not die with the building. The nuns cross the Rhine to the daughter house she founded in her sixties, and take her with them.
suggested_refs: The surviving Rupertsberg cellar vault at Bingerbrück

stops.name: Eibingen, the bones cross the river
stops.date_confidence: the outcome is attested; the chain of custody across the 1632 destruction and the 1803 secularization is not documented in detail, and the sources describing it have an interest in its being unbroken
stops.campa: Her bones are brought over the Rhine to Eibingen, the second house, and set in a shrine there. They stay through the secularization of 1803, which dissolves the convent and sells the buildings; the parish buys the church in 1831, and the reliquary stays because the parish now owns the room it stands in. The detailed custody across two centuries of fire and confiscation is not documented. Pilgrims have come to the Eibingen shrine for four hundred years regardless.
sources: Abtei St. Hildegard, Eibingen, community history
suggested_refs: The reliquary shrine of St. Hildegard in the parish church at Eibingen

stops.name: Eibingen, the abbey rebuilt and the codex copied by hand
stops.date_confidence: the abbey was founded 2 July 1900 and occupied 17 September 1904 by twelve Benedictine nuns; the painted facsimile of the Scivias was made 1927-1933
stops.campa: On the hill above Eibingen a new Benedictine abbey is built between 1900 and 1904, and twelve nuns move in on the seventeenth of September, her death day. In its scriptorium, between 1927 and 1933, the sisters make a hand-painted copy of the Rupertsberg Scivias codex, page for page, colour for colour. They finish twelve years before the original vanishes into a burning city. Every colour reproduction of her visions printed since comes from their copy.
sources: Abtei St. Hildegard, Eibingen, official community history
suggested_refs: The 1927-1933 Eibingen facsimile of the Scivias illuminations

stops.name: Dresden, the codex does not come back
stops.date_confidence: attested as lost; the manuscript's own production is dated by Wikipedia to around the time of her death, c.1175-1180, and prepared under her supervision or that of her immediate tradition, a hedge the research pool dropped
stops.campa: The illuminated Scivias, made at the Rupertsberg around the time of her death, has been in the library at Wiesbaden for centuries. In the war it is sent to Dresden for safekeeping. It does not come back. The thirty-five images go with it. The only reason the visions can still be looked at by anyone is that a house of nuns spent six years copying them by hand, in the untroubled belief that the original would always be there and the copy was merely for their own use.
suggested_refs: The lost Rupertsberg Scivias codex, last recorded at Dresden

stops.name: Vatican City, Doctor of the Church
stops.date_confidence: attested. The medieval record is contested: four popes opened processes between 1228 and the 1330s and none concluded, though John XXII confirmed her cult on 26 August 1326. The 1584 date given for her entry in the Roman Martyrology was not confirmed.
stops.campa: Four popes opened inquiries into her canonization and none of them finished. A cult confirmation was issued in 1326, and for six centuries afterward she was a saint by usage rather than by decree, kept in the Martyrology and in the calendars of Mainz, Trier, Speyer, and Limburg. In May 2012 Benedict XVI extends her cult to the whole Church by equivalent canonization. In October he names her a Doctor of the Church, one of four women then holding the title.
suggested_refs: Benedict XVI, apostolic letter proclaiming Hildegard a Doctor of the Universal Church, 7 October 2012
